title: The temple built in a mind
hook: a poor devotee builds Shiva a temple no one can see, and Shiva goes there first
carry: worship offered in the mind is real worship
tomorrow: an unfinished god, worshipped by millions. what made him holy?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sri Yantra rose off the page into the Meru: the holy sits at the center; the ego bows. Today the yantra travels somewhere stranger.

The Periya Puranam, the lives of the Tamil saints of Shiva, tells of a poor devotee named Pusalar who longs to build Shiva a temple. He has no money for stone. So he builds it in his mind: the foundation, the walls, the tower, piece by piece, day after day, for a long time. When it's finished, he fixes an auspicious day to consecrate it. On that same day, the Pallava king at Kanchi is consecrating his own great stone temple. The night before, Shiva comes to the king in a dream. Wait, he says. Tomorrow I'm going to Pusalar's temple.
screen: `NO MONEY FOR STONE.` → `HE BUILDS IT IN HIS MIND.` → `SHIVA: TOMORROW I'M GOING TO PUSALAR'S.`

segments.voice: The king travels to Pusalar's town to see this rival temple. There's nothing there. He finds Pusalar and asks where it stands. Pusalar, amazed that Shiva noticed him at all, tells him: inside. Built of devotion, not stone. And the king bows to him. Hindus have a name for what Pusalar did: manasa puja, worship offered in the mind. Every part of an ordinary puja, the bath, the flowers, the lamp, the food, can be offered inwardly, and the tradition treats it as real worship, not a lesser copy. In the story, Shiva went to the inner temple first. That's the part worth telling a friend tonight. Sri Vidya, the worship of the Goddess through the Sri Yantra, takes this the furthest. A short text called the Bhavana Upanishad, bhavana meaning contemplation, lines up the yantra's layers with the worshipper's own body, senses and mind. In that text the worshipper isn't only looking at the map. The worshipper is the map. None of this throws out stone temples or the brass yantra. Most families worship outwardly and inwardly both, and lineages weigh the two differently. But it means worship can't be taken from you. Picture a woman on a long flight, her yantra left on her altar at home. At her usual hour she closes her eyes, and her lips start to move. Nothing is missing. Pusalar would understand.
screen: `A TEMPLE OF DEVOTION, NOT STONE.` · `MANASA PUJA: WORSHIP IN THE MIND.` · `SHIVA WENT THERE FIRST.` · `THE BHAVANA UPANISHAD: THE WORSHIPPER IS THE MAP.` · then, large: `WORSHIP NO ONE CAN TAKE FROM YOU.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and close your eyes. Picture your altar, or any shrine you love, in detail. In your mind, offer one flower, then light one lamp, slowly, the way Pusalar set one stone at a time. If you don't pray, picture one beautiful thing instead and hold it steady until the sit ends.
The Sri Yantra: the Goddess's diagram, which the Bhavana Upanishad reads onto the worshipper's own body, senses and mind, so it can be worshipped within.
Your line: worship offered in the mind is real worship. Pusalar's temple had no stone, and Shiva went there first. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Manasa puja, worship offered in the mind, is a recognized form of Hindu worship. In Sri Vidya some practitioners worship the Sri Yantra outwardly with flowers and kumkum, some inwardly as the Bhavana Upanishad describes, and many do both; lineages weigh the two differently.
